briefing.text: Meridian Holdings. We go in the front — the storefront admin. Get inside, map what's back there, and walk out with the first score. Three moves: the door, the floor plan, the manifest.

objectives.why: The admin console is the door to everything else in Meridian.
objectives.doneWhen: A row with is_admin = 1 comes back — you're logged in as staff.
objectives.approach: The login only checks the text you hand it. Treat the username box as a way to rewrite the QUESTION the database asks — not just a name — and you can walk in as staff without ever knowing the password.

query.template: SELECT id, username, is_admin FROM users WHERE username = '{{input:username}}' AND password = '{{input:password}}'

winCondition.reason: Privileged account pulled - the front door is open, you're in.

hints.text: The lock only checks what you hand it. What if what you hand it isn't just a name — what if it closes the quote and changes the question?
Two ideas: make the condition always true (OR plus an equality that is always true), or cut the line short with --. A quote can end the string early.
In the username, try  admin' --   or  ' OR '1'='1' -- . The trailing -- comments out the password check.

expectedSolution.note: Alternative: username  admin' --   also wins; the trailing -- comments out the password check.

debrief.explanation: Your input is concatenated straight into the SQL string, so a closing quote stops being data and becomes code: it ends the username string early, and the trailing -- comments out the rest of the statement, including the password check. The always-true OR '1'='1' then matches every row.

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - username/password interpolated straight into the SQL string
cur.execute(
    f"SELECT id, username, is_admin FROM users "
    f"WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'"
)
row = cur.fetchone()
# psycopg2 %-format is the same flaw: "... username = '%s'" % username

Java (JDBC)
C# / .NET (ADO.NET)
Go (database/sql)
Ruby on Rails (ActiveRecord)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - username/password interpolated straight into the SQL string
user = User.where(
  "username = '#{username}' AND password = '#{password}'"
).first
# find_by_sql is just as unsafe: User.find_by_sql("... username = '#{username}'")

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Laravel (Query Builder)
Django (ORM)
vulnerableCodeVariants.code:
# VULNERABLE - input interpolated into raw SQL, bypassing the ORM's binding
user = User.objects.raw(
    f"SELECT id, username, is_admin FROM users "
    f"WHERE username = '{username}' AND password = '{password}'"
)[0]
# .extra(where=[f"username = '{username}'"]) is just as unsafe

vulnerableCodeVariants.label: Spring Boot (JdbcTemplate)

secureCodeVariants.label: Node.js (pg / mysql2)
Python (sqlite3 / psycopg2)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# sqlite3 — ? placeholders are bound; input is never parsed as SQL
cur.execute(
    "SELECT id, username, is_admin FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?",
    (username, password),
)
row = cur.fetchone()
# psycopg2 uses %s: cur.execute("... username = %s AND password = %s", (username, password))

Java (JDBC)
C# / .NET (ADO.NET)
Go (database/sql)
Ruby on Rails (ActiveRecord)

secureCodeVariants.label: Laravel (Query Builder)
Django (ORM)
secureCodeVariants.code:
# Django ORM — every lookup value is parameterized automatically
user = User.objects.filter(
    username=username, password=password
).first()
# .raw() still binds: User.objects.raw("... WHERE username = %s", [username])

secureCodeVariants.label: Spring Boot (JdbcTemplate)

debrief.takeaway: Stop gluing what people type onto your questions. Bind it — and "or one equals one" is just a bad username again.

payoff.fixer: Admin's badge on your chest. Now we can walk the whole floor plan — find what they don't list.

objectives.goal: List the rooms Meridian keeps off its own floor plan.
objectives.why: You can't rob a room you can't name — read the building's own index and find what recon never listed.
objectives.doneWhen: The catalog hands back a table recon never showed you.
objectives.approach: Recon only lists part of the database. The room you're after isn't on that map — so first make the database hand over its own list of tables, then read the hidden one recon never showed you.

query.template: SELECT title, body FROM articles WHERE title LIKE '%{{input:q}}%'

winCondition.reason: The catalog gave up a hidden room — offshore_accounts, a table recon never listed.

hints.text: You've got the trick from the Vault. What you don't have is the room number. Stop guessing — the building keeps a list of its own rooms. Ask it for that list first.
Do not guess the table name - the database keeps its own catalog: sqlite_master. Pull name and sql; the sql column shows the columns. This job is 2 columns.
The articles search returns 2 columns, so match it:  ' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master --   The name column lists every table — including offshore_accounts, the room you rob next.

inputs.q: ' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master --

expectedSolution.note: The catalog read returns every table's name and its CREATE — including the two rooms recon hid (z_bp_registry_7f3a and offshore_accounts). Those names are what the next objective needs.

debrief.explanation: You don't know the hidden table's name, so you read the database's own catalog — sqlite_master — through the UNION. Its rows list every table plus the CREATE statement that spells out each one's columns. The app query returns 2 columns, so the UNION must supply exactly 2 (here name and sql). That index is the only place offshore_accounts is written down — recon never listed it.

)
rows = cur.fetchall()
# UNION / sqlite_master ride straight in through the unclosed quote.

payoff.fixer: Two rooms they keep off the floor plan — a blueprint cache and an offshore ledger. Names in hand, we can reach straight into the ledger.

objectives.goal: Pull the offshore ledger you just mapped off the shopping page.
objectives.why: You have its name now — offshore_accounts, the room recon hid. That account is the first score.
objectives.doneWhen: The vault manifest tag shows up in the result grid.
objectives.approach: You mapped a hidden ledger of accounts a step ago. This product search only hands back one shape of answer — ride a second question out on the same channel to pull that hidden table's rows onto the page.

query.template: SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{{input:q}}%'

winCondition.reason: Vault manifest surfaced in the result grid - the cross-table UNION held.

hints.text: The room isn't on the floor plan — you mapped its name a step ago. First learn how wide this search is: how many columns come back, so a second question can ride out on the same tray.
First find how many columns come back: ORDER BY 1, 2, 3 ... until it breaks; the last one that works is the count. Then UNION SELECT that many values - the second query must match the column count.
It is 3 columns. Try  ' UNION SELECT holder_name, account_ref, balance_usd FROM offshore_accounts --

inputs.q: ' UNION SELECT holder_name, account_ref, balance_usd FROM offshore_accounts --

expectedSolution.note: First the column count:  ' ORDER BY 3 --   is OK,  ' ORDER BY 4 --   errors => 3 columns.

debrief.explanation: The search term is concatenated into the LIKE pattern, so a closing quote ends the search string and lets you append UNION SELECT. UNION staples a second query - from an unrelated table - onto the same result set; the only requirement is a matching column count, which is why the recon step is discovering that the query returns 3 columns.
